sources.title:
10K views · 237 reactions | On November 13, 2025, Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket successfully launched NASA's ESCAPADE mission from Launch Complex 36 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, marking the vehicle's second flight after weather and solar activity delays from earlier attempts. The heavy-lift rocket, standing over 320 feet tall and powered by seven BE-4 methane-fueled engines on its reusable first stage, lifted off at 3:55 p.m. EST, carrying twin small spacecraft—Blue and Gold—built by Rocket Lab for the University of California, Berkeley, to study Mars' magnetosphere, solar wind interactions, and atmospheric escape processes. Approximately 33 minutes after liftoff, the satellites deployed into a trajectory for a Mars arrival in 2026, while the first-stage booster, named "Never Tell Me The Odds," executed a series of burns and landed upright on Blue Origin's Atlantic Ocean droneship Jacklyn for the first time, validating the company's reusability goals and positioning New Glenn as a competitor to SpaceX's Falcon Heavy for NASA science payloads at a cost of about $18 million.
Video by Dennis Hlavsa / @dhlavsa with Space FrontPage and Launch Window Photo 

 #BlueOrigin #NASA #spaceexploration #rockelaunch #RocketLaunchViews #NewGlenn #escapade | Space FrontPage

24K views · 439 reactions | On September 24, 2025, NASA successfully launched the Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP), along with two secondary spacecraft, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. The mission's primary objective is to map the boundaries of the heliosphere, the giant protective bubble created by the solar wind that shields our solar system from harmful cosmic radiation.

Launch and deployment details

Launch vehicle: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launched from Launch Complex 39A at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Liftoff: The mission lifted off on Wednesday, September 24, 2025, at 7:30 a.m. EDT.

Rideshare payloads: In addition to IMAP, the rocket also carried NOAA's Space Weather Follow On-Lagrange 1 (SWFO-L1) and NASA's Carruthers Geocorona Observatory.

Orbital destination: All three spacecraft are traveling to the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange Point, a gravitationally stable position approximately 1 million miles from Earth. They are expected to arrive in January 2026.

Signal acquisition: IMAP successfully established communications with mission control shortly after its deployment from the rocket's second stage.

Booster landing: The Falcon 9 first-stage booster successfully landed on the droneship "Just Read the Instructions" in the Atlantic Ocean.

Dennis Hlavsa /@dhlavsa with Space FrontPage and Launch Window Photo 

#NASA #SpaceX #falcon9 #IMAP #launchvideo #NOAA | Space FrontPage

excerpts.text: ESCAPADE is expected to launch no earlier than Nov. 9, 2025, on the second mission of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket. After taking off from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida, the probes will travel to a holding position and remain there for about a year while studying space weather near Earth.

ESCAPADE was originally expected to launch as a rideshare with NASA’s [Psyche](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/psyche) mission in 2022, but when NASA decided to launch Psyche on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, ESCAPADE could not be updated in time to take into account the more energetic orbit such a launch would result in.
